content: Eye injuries, whether physical or chemical, can pose a significant threat to vision if not managed promptly and appropriately. The most common signs of ocular injuries include redness and pain in the affected eye. However, this is not always the case, as small metallic projectiles may not produce these symptoms. Such projectiles should be suspected when a patient reports incidents involving metal-on-metal contact, such as hammering a metal surface. Intraocular foreign bodies often do not cause pain because the vitreous humor and retina lack nerve endings capable of transmitting pain sensations. Therefore, general or emergency room physicians should refer cases involving the posterior segment of the eye or intraocular foreign bodies to an ophthalmologist. It is preferable to avoid using ointments before referring the patient, as they can interfere with a comprehensive eye examination. Eye trauma is frequently caused by flying debris such as wood, metal, glass, stone, or other materials. Blunt injuries from objects like fists (e.g., during physical altercations), sports balls (e.g., cricket or tennis balls), shuttlecocks (e.g., from badminton), or other high-speed projectiles can also result in significant ocular damage. Children may sustain eye injuries from activities such as playing with bows and arrows or firecrackers, particularly during festivals like Dussehra and Diwali in India. Road traffic accidents involving head and facial trauma often include severe eye injuries, which may present with multiple lacerations, embedded glass shards, orbital fractures, extensive hematomas, or penetrating open-globe injuries with prolapse of ocular contents. Workplace tools and even common household implements can also lead to intraocular trauma. A study conducted between 2002 and 2003 in the United States estimated 27,152 eye injuries related to eyeglass wear. The study found that sports-related injuries involving eyeglasses were more common in individuals under 18 years of age, while fall-related injuries were more prevalent in those aged 65 or older. Despite the occurrence of eyeglass-related injuries, both prescription eyeglasses and non-prescription sunglasses have been shown to provide measurable protection, reducing the incidence of severe eye injuries among wearers. Eye injuries can lead to numerous complications, including corneal scarring, hyphema, iridodialysis, post-traumatic glaucoma, uveitis, cataracts, vitreous hemorrhage, and retinal detachment. The risk of complications is particularly high in cases involving retinal tears, penetrating injuries, and severe blunt trauma.
